solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Short Biblical book to appraise

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the book's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Judges is a book of the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A request to give a brief assessment of one of the books of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: To appraise something is to assess or form an opinion of it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Jack, an A.A. Milne character, dropping round for book

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards
taken as written

indicators.note: dropping means letting fall, so the round letter leaves the character's name

parts.note: Eeyore is the gloomy donkey in Winnie-the-Pooh
a round shape is a circle, the letter O

explanation.surface: A boy named Jack and a Milne character have somehow lost something round, all to do with a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a boy's name but is the card abbreviation; 'dropping' takes the round letter out of the donkey's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte Brontë's novel of the governess at Thornfield, so an example of a book.

clue.text: Awkward deadline concerning upcoming English novelist

indicators.note: awkward suggests the letters of the word are clumsily arranged and need sorting

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: of means concerning, as in 'tales of the sea'

explanation.surface: An English novelist faces an awkward deadline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awkward' turns DEADLINE into DANIELDE; 'upcoming' turns OF into FO.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Robinson Crusoe and Moll Flanders is a famous English writer of fiction.

clue.text: Last in tabernacle, you say, about to record parting words?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the final letters go round the record
last in tells us to take the final letter of each of the following words

parts.note: to log something is to record it

explanation.surface: A question about recording a farewell spoken in a place of worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'you, say' looks like a sound-alike signal, but it simply supplies the last letter U, as 'say' supplies Y. The finals E, U, Y wrap LOG.
explanation.definitionFit: A funeral tribute is a speech of praise given as the deceased departs, hence words at a parting.

clue.text: Physician with House in TV series?

parts.note: a physician is a doctor
HO is the abbreviation for house, as in addresses

explanation.surface: Dr Gregory House, the medic of the TV show House, seems to be what is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: Mentioning House, the American medical drama, invites thinking of that series; it is just the abbreviation HO.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-running BBC science fiction programme about a time-travelling Time Lord.

clue.text: Suspect provides name shown to be false

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means dubious, hinting that the letters are not in their proper order

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A suspect supplies a name, which turns out to be a lie.
explanation.definitionFit: A refuted claim has been demonstrated to be untrue, so the past participle fits exactly.

clue.text: Chapter on pike leaves one cold

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above the next piece

parts.note: a pike is a pointed hill or peak, especially in the Lake District

explanation.surface: A chapter about a pike, the fish, leaves the reader unmoved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pike' suggests the fish, but in northern England a pike is a peaked hill.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold, the minor illness, is also called a chill.

clue.text: Old British ruined castle, a stumbling block

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the word's letters are knocked into a new arrangement

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An old British castle lies in ruins, getting in someone's way.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstruction or hindrance in one's path is a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Misery caused by wife, heartless one

indicators.note: heartless means the middle letter of the word is cut out, leaving its ends

explanation.surface: A cruel spouse brings unhappiness to the household.
explanation.definitionFit: Woe is great sorrow or distress, a direct synonym of misery.

clue.text: Fair article supporting knight entering exam

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so the pair goes into the exam

parts.note: an O level was the former British exam taken at about sixteen

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting means placed below the piece it holds up

parts.note: N is knight in chess notation
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A grammatical article holding up a knight who is sitting an exam, which seems fair.
explanation.walkthrough: O LEVEL was the British school exam taken at about sixteen before the GCSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Being honest and straightforward is to be fair and above board, an idiom.

clue.text: Completely perplex last of men on bonus

indicators.note: last of means take the final letter of the word men

parts.note: a plus is an advantage or bonus

explanation.surface: The final word on a bonus scheme leaves the staff completely baffled.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewilder someone so thoroughly they cannot respond; nonplus is a verb meaning to baffle.

clue.text: Study foremost of protocols in cricket, perhaps

indicators.note: in means the letter is placed inside the creature

parts.note: a cricket is an example of an insect, flagged by perhaps

indicators.note: foremost of means the first letter of protocols

explanation.surface: Studying the main protocols of the game of cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cricket' suggests the sport, but here it is the chirping insect.
explanation.definitionFit: To inspect is to examine closely, a verb sense of study.

clue.text: Everyone inside read page on artful writer of short stories

indicators.note: inside means the group goes within the rearranged letters
artful means crafty or cunningly arranged, signalling a reshuffle

parts.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder
all means everyone

explanation.surface: Everyone reads a page about a crafty author of tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'artful' seems to describe the writer's style, yet it signals the jumble of the middle words; 'inside' places the word for everyone within that result.
explanation.definitionFit: The American master of macabre tales such as The Tell-Tale Heart is a famous short story writer.

clue.text: Hack writer nearly going crazy stopping at home

parts.note: a pen is something to write with

indicators.note: stopping means plugging a gap, so the word for home goes into the jumble
going crazy suggests the letters are scrambled

parts.note: anagram fodder
in means at home, as in 'staying in'

explanation.surface: A writer who has nearly gone mad from being stuck indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going crazy' turns NEARLY into NYALER, which IN stops to make NYALINER.
explanation.definitionFit: A penny-a-liner was a hack paid by the line, so a poorly paid journalist.

clue.text: Place for shabby writers to eat on the way?

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above the next piece

parts.note: to grub is slang for to eat
a street is a way or road

explanation.surface: Somewhere down-at-heel authors might grab a bite while travelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A London street once home to needy hack authors, now a name for literary hackdom.

clue.text: Narrator's identity concealed by Blackmore, initially?

definitions.note: the 's reads as 'is', so the narrator is what the wordplay makes

indicators.note: concealed by means hidden inside, so the initials go around the identity

parts.note: R.D. Blackmore, the author of Lorna Doone, had the initials R and D
ID is short for identity

explanation.surface: A narrator's real identity is hidden by the novelist Blackmore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' looks like a first-letter signal, but it means the author's own initials.
explanation.definitionFit: John Ridd is the storyteller of Blackmore's Lorna Doone, so an example of a narrator.

clue.text: Canon, note, breaking bad habit — bitter hostility results

indicators.note: breaking means breaking into, so the pair splits the bad habit

parts.note: a vice is a bad habit
a canon is a rule or principle
N is short for note, as in an IOU or banknote

explanation.surface: A churchman and a written note interrupt a bad habit, with hostility following.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canon' suggests a clergyman, but it is a rule.
explanation.definitionFit: Virulence means extreme bitterness or malice, as well as the potency of a disease.

clue.text: Dramatist ran hostel in resort

indicators.note: resort read as re-sort means sort again, so the letters are reshuffled

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A playwright managed a holiday hostel at the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday town but is read as re-sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack Rosenthal was a British television playwright, so an example of a dramatist.

clue.text: No longer married, man with church housed by theologian?

indicators.note: housed by means held inside, so the theologian goes around the pair

parts.note: DD stands for Doctor of Divinity
Ivor is a man's name
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A man and his church lodged with a theologian, now separated from his wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone whose marriage has been legally ended is a divorcee, so no longer wed.

clue.text: Favours live US sitcom

parts.note: to be is to exist or live
Friends was a long-running American situation comedy

explanation.surface: Fans of a live recording of an American comedy show.
explanation.definitionFit: To befriend someone is to help or support them, which is to show them favour.

clue.text: Intensive publicity could get one over-excited, briefly

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: hyper is slang for over-excited

explanation.surface: A media blitz could get someone overwrought.
explanation.definitionFit: Hype is extravagant promotion or a publicity blitz in the media.

clue.text: Capital city's lighter beneath moon? Not half!

indicators.note: in a down clue, beneath means the vessel goes below
not half means only half the word is kept, its first two letters

parts.note: a scow is a flat-bottomed barge, a kind of lighter

explanation.surface: A city's lamp shining under the moon, with an exclamation of agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lighter' suggests a cigarette lighter, but it is a barge for loading ships. 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so'.
explanation.definitionFit: Moscow is the seat of Russia's government, so an example of a capital city.

clue.text: Who let loose about successful book (novel)?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the middle pair
let loose suggests letters set free to fall into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder
golden means successful, as in a golden period

explanation.surface: Someone asks who unleashed a book about success.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed '(novel)' is the definition; 'loose' shuffles the first two words, and 'about' wraps that jumble round the middle pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry James's late novel about a flawed gilded crystal bowl, an example of a novel.

clue.text: Hot inside food shop in Indian city

indicators.note: inside means the letter goes within the shop

parts.note: a deli is a delicatessen
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Hot food served in a shop in an Indian city.
explanation.definitionFit: Delhi is the city that contains New Delhi, the capital of India.

clue.text: See 1
Conforming to accepted standards, I teach New Latin?

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so these letters are put in a fresh order

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A teacher wonders whether teaching New Latin is morally proper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Latin' looks like the scholarly language; 'New' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethical means morally right, in line with accepted principles of conduct.

clue.text: Methuen's view

indicators.note: the possessive 's says the view belongs to, and is held within, the publisher's name

explanation.surface: The opinion of the publisher Methuen.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive signals the letters belong to Methuen's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hue can mean aspect or appearance, the look of something as seen.

clue.text: Artist shows opener for Northants in game

indicators.note: in means the letter goes inside the game

parts.note: hockey is a field game

indicators.note: opener for means the first letter of Northants

explanation.surface: A painter shows up to open the batting for Northamptonshire's team.
explanation.walkthrough: Northants is short for Northamptonshire, an English county; 'opener' hints at cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: David Hockney is a celebrated British painter, an example of an artist.

clue.text: Time to study factory's exercise machine

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it at university
a mill is a factory, the 's linking it to the answer

explanation.surface: Time to look into the factory's gym equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: A moving belt to walk or run on, a gym apparatus.

clue.text: Publisher, new in Hertfordshire town

indicators.note: in means the letter goes inside the town

parts.note: Ware is a market town in Hertfordshire, England

explanation.surface: A publisher opening up in a Hertfordshire town.
explanation.definitionFit: Frederick Warne & Co published Beatrix Potter's books, so an example of a publisher.
